title: NOAA Atlas 15 Informational Page
key_claim: NOAA Atlas 15 represents a shift from a stationary assumption to a nonstationary assumption in national precipitation-frequency standards; preliminary estimates for the contiguous US will be released for peer review by September 2026, with publication in 2027, superseding NOAA Atlas 14, which is referenced in many engineering design standards and floodplain regulations.
frame_summary: NOAA argues that US precipitation-frequency design standards must move from a stationary to a nonstationary statistical basis to remain authoritative as the climate changes.
verbatim_quote: a shift from a stationary assumption (i.e., extreme precipitation events do not change significantly over time) to a nonstationary assumption (i.e., extreme precipitation events change over time)
notes: Evergreen NOAA programme/info page. Anchor for the US methodological pivot. CONUS preliminary estimates by September 2026 per the page's News box.

publisher: Environment Agency / Defra Data Services Platform
title: Climate Change Data (Flood Map for Planning)
key_claim: For surface-water spatial planning datasets in the Flood Map for Planning, the Environment Agency now uses the 'upper end' (95th percentile) allowance for the 2070s epoch (2061 to 2125); for rivers and sea it uses central 2080s and upper-end 95th-percentile sea-level allowances to 2125.
frame_summary: The Environment Agency argues that statutory flood-planning datasets must be rebased onto upper-end, late-century climate allowances rather than mid-century central scenarios.
verbatim_quote: the 'upper end' (95th percentile) allowance for the 2070s epoch (2061 to 2125)
notes: Page updated 28 May 2026 (visible Created/Updated line). Core UK regulatory anchor for the design-basis shift.

title: British way of life under threat from heat, flooding and drought (A Well-Adapted UK, CCRA4-IA)
key_claim: By 2050, 92% of homes are likely to overheat, peak river flows will be up to 45% higher and water supply shortfalls could exceed five billion litres a day; adaptation requires investment of around GBP 11 billion a year; without adaptation the cost to public welfare rises to 1-5% of UK GDP by 2050 (GBP 60-260 billion a year); the report calls to adapt infrastructure to operate safely under future climate conditions.
frame_summary: The CCC argues the UK is dangerously underprepared and that transport, energy and other infrastructure must be designed and maintained to operate under future, not historical, climate conditions.
notes: CCC fourth Independent Assessment of UK Climate Risk. Tier 1 statutory advisory body.

title: Adaptation and insurance: strategies to narrow the protection gap (sigma 1/2026)
date_evidence: Press Release 92% of losses driven by natural disasters 19 Mar 2026; Nat Cat sigma 1/2026
key_claim: More than 40% of global natural-catastrophe losses are now insured (up from 23% thirty years ago) but 80-90% of losses remain uninsured in many emerging markets; UK household flood losses would be 2.8 times higher without existing defences, per Swiss Re's Fathom water-risk unit.
frame_summary: Swiss Re argues that adaptation and insurance must be scaled together because exposure is outpacing protection and existing defences were built for a different climate.
notes: sigma 1/2026 natcat report, press release 19 Mar 2026. Treated as the single structural anchor in the 3-6 month band (canonical natcat protection-gap reference).

title: The climate threat is worsening, but a well-adapted UK is within reach, says the CCC
date_evidence: Date 20 May 2026 ... a 'critical window' for engineers to ensure those new assets are well-adapted
key_claim: ICE frames the government's 10-year infrastructure strategy as a 'critical window' for engineers to design new assets to future climate conditions, says promised resilience standards will be crucial to set consistent benchmarks, and cites cascading-failure risk illustrated by the North Hyde substation fire that closed Heathrow; keeping flood risk at today's level needs GBP 1.6-2.2 billion a year of investment to 2050.
frame_summary: ICE argues that engineers and government must use the current infrastructure-investment cycle to lock in forward-looking resilience standards, or risk building new assets to obsolete climate baselines.
notes: ICE Inside Infrastructure analysis of the CCC report, 20 May 2026. Engineering-profession voice on standards.

publisher: Levy Economics Institute of Bard College
title: A Premium Crisis: Climate Change Threatens Homeowner's Insurance, Housing, and Financial Stability (Policy Note 2026/2)
key_claim: US home-insurance premiums rose 41.4% over 2020-2024 (far above 22.5% cumulative CPI inflation); the share of uninsured homeowners more than doubled from 5% to 12% between 2015 and 2023; premiums rose from 7-8% of mortgage costs in 2013 to 20% in 2022; FSOC has identified climate change as an emerging threat to US financial stability and Fed Chair Powell warned some regions may become un-mortgageable.
frame_summary: The Levy Institute argues that climate-driven insurance repricing and withdrawal is transmitting into mortgage and housing-finance risk and is a systemic threat to US financial stability.
notes: Levy Policy Note 2026/2. Source for the financial-transmission (insurance to mortgage) leg of the signal.

title: Using Extreme Engineering to Flood-Proof Coastal Cities
date_evidence: Bloomberg Articles (May 20, 2026): 'Using Extreme Engineering to Flood-Proof Coastal Cities' explores how global capitals from Tokyo to Jakarta and Nairobi are grappling with increasingly dangerous weather
key_claim: Cities from Tokyo to Jakarta to Nairobi are turning to large-scale flood-engineering retrofits as defences built for past conditions prove inadequate to current weather, signalling a global wave of adaptation spending.
frame_summary: Bloomberg reports that major world cities are spending heavily on extreme flood-engineering because existing infrastructure was built for a climate that has already shifted.
notes: Quality-journalism corroboration for global scope; paywalled, used directionally only, not as a quantitative anchor.
